source.title: Automated Neuron Labelling Enables Generative Steering and Interpretability in Protein Language Models
source.authors: Arjun Banerjee; David Martinez; Camille Dang; Ethan Tam

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present. The text contains some inconsistent model names and sizes, noted under problems.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses neuron labels as a tool for steering protein generation and reports steering outcomes. It does not measure the share of neurons with one or two jobs, test explanation accuracy with reported held-out scores, or test the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper does not report an audit of neuron-pole job counts or a percentage of labels that are accurate. It describes a held-out simulator and uses it to select explanations, but reports no simulator correlations or other results evaluating explanation quality. Illustrative labels in Table 1 are not an audit of their accuracy. Rows below record outcomes from neuron steering and the paper's reported scaling observations; these do not test a listed version. Cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study labels ESM protein-model neurons with GPT-4.1-nano and a Longformer simulator, then uses the labels to steer generation. It reports no share of neurons with one or two jobs and no simulator correlation scores. It has no InceptionV1, attribution-graph or explanation-fidelity results. Its own results are steering outcomes and qualitative layer distributions, so it bears on no version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The authors claim a scalable neuron-labelling and steering framework for PLMs and preliminary scaling observations. They acknowledge possibly oversimplified or hallucinated labels and non-viable folding.
record.recipe_differences: The study labels protein-language-model neurons from top-activating protein examples using GPT-4.1-nano explanations and a Longformer simulator, then intervenes on neuron activations for protein generation. It does not audit positive and negative neuron poles or estimate single-job shares.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported effects depend on target feature and steering direction: negative steering completely inverted positive steering for GRAVY, gave no conclusive direction for instability index, and increased molecular weight for both low- and high-molecular-weight targets. The characteristic-steering figures also use different affine parameters for esm2 t12 35M and esm2 t6 8M.

fits_no_version.finding: Label-guided neuron activation steering shifted molecular weight, GRAVY and instability index in ESM2 8M/35M. Results were mixed under negative steering. Secondary-structure and zinc-finger targeting was incomplete (1/100 fully correct zinc fingers), and generated proteins likely do not fold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron labels in protein language models can serve as a control interface for steering generated-sequence properties, with property-dependent reliability.

fits_no_version.finding: Labelled feature categories follow a sequence-to-structure-to-function layer progression. Larger ESM models show finer structural labels and earlier functional labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In ESM2, neuron labels show hierarchical layer organization that shifts with model size.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the Workshop on Generative AI for Biology at ICML 2025, PMLR 267
record.problems: The paper reports no numeric held-out simulator correlations, no human evaluation of label quality, and no quantified share of labels or neurons that are accurate or single-feature. The authors themselves note possible oversimplified or hallucinated explanations and that generated proteins may not fold viably. Model naming is inconsistent: the interpretability section repeats esm2 t36 8B UR50D in its list of three models, while the scaling discussion and figures refer to ESM-8M, ESM-35M, ESM-3B, and 8B variants.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-relevant findings were omitted. Generated-protein ΔG calculations and dataset-distribution plots were not included as rows because they do not measure neuron interpretation or neuron-steering effects on the listed claims. Table 1's illustrative neuron descriptions were not treated as tested explanation outcomes.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or job-count shares.
Protein LMs at several sizes are labelled, but no share of single-job or interpretable neurons is reported for any of them.
No interpretable-share estimates across tools or architectures. The authors' attribution of late specialization to capacity bottlenecks is speculation, not a measured share.
No attribution graphs or replacement-model comparison.
A held-out simulator is described, but no fidelity results comparing explanations with held-out activations are reported.
Simulator Pearson correlations are computed only to rank hypotheses; no scores or share of well-scored neurons are reported.

record.verdict_notes: The record cites Bills et al. (an original source) only as background. The simulator is used for selection, not reported as an evaluation. The control row r20 gives no model and no metric values. Model-name inconsistencies in Section 4 (repeated 'esm2 t36 8B') make the scaling subjects uncertain.

versions.untested_parts: No Qwen3-32B audit, neuron-pole counts, or one-job/two-job/ununderstood shares.

The paper labels neurons in protein language models at several sizes, but does not measure whether the claimed neuron-pole shares hold across models, dense/MoE architectures, or up to trillions of parameters.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose analysis, or test of recursive generalization versus superposition.

The paper reports qualitative differences in features identified across ESM sizes, but does not estimate shares of interpretable neurons or test the stated InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates or causal roles for architecture, regularization, and tools.
No attribution graphs, reconstruction error, or test of whether neuron-based graphs explain behavior without a replacement model.
The paper describes a simulator for held-out sequences but reports no results showing whether explanations that fit activating examples fail to predict activation on new examples.
No reported automated explanation scores or share of neurons achieving good scores.

rows.subject: esm2 t12 35M
rows.operation_detail: Applied negative steering to neurons associated with GRAVY score.
rows.measure: GRAVY score response relative to positive steering
rows.baseline: positive steering result; numeric value not stated
rows.value: Negative steering produced the complete inverse result of positive steering.
rows.note: The paper says this relationship was feature dependent.

rows.subject: esm2 t12 35M
rows.operation_detail: Applied negative steering to neurons associated with instability index.
rows.baseline: positive steering result; numeric value not stated
rows.value: No conclusive direction changes were observed.
rows.note: The text reports an inconclusive direction rather than a clear null effect.

rows.subject: esm2 t12 35M
rows.operation_detail: Applied negative steering to neurons associated with high molecular weight.
rows.baseline: positive steering result; numeric value not stated
rows.value: Negative steering of both high- and low-molecular-weight targets increased molecular weight.
rows.note: The text does not give the expected direction or a numeric comparison for this individual target.

rows.subject: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Steered a randomly initialized sequence toward alpha-helical structure using selected neurons.

conditions.value: neutral sequence of 75 D-configuration amino acids

rows.baseline: neutral starting sequence; numeric result not stated
rows.value: The alpha-steered protein had 5 distinct alpha-helix domains spanning 34% of the protein and also 3 beta-strand domains.
rows.note: The paper also says generated proteins were unlikely to fold viably; the target and opposing motifs are both reported here.
rows.check: Subject is not stated. Section 3 says generation used esm2 t6 8M and esm2 t12 35M but does not say which model this row used. The row is a steering outcome, not a neuron-interpretability measure.

rows.subject: ESM-3B
rows.operation_detail: Compared labeled structural features across model sizes and layer sextiles.
rows.measure: Structural features identified in neuron labels
rows.baseline: ESM-8M comparison; exact values not stated
rows.value: The paper reports that ESM-3B captured details including hands, supercoiling, and fingers.
rows.note: This is a qualitative scaling observation, not a measure of the share of interpretable neurons.
rows.check: This is a qualitative label-content comparison read from a figure, not a measured effect. The text also lists inconsistent model names (repeated 'esm2 t36 8B'), so subject identity is uncertain. The state 'observed' has no version effect to anchor it.

rows.subject: ESM-8M
rows.operation_detail: Compared labeled structural features across model sizes and layer sextiles.
rows.measure: Structural features identified in neuron labels
rows.baseline: ESM-3B comparison; exact values not stated
rows.value: The paper reports that ESM-8M captured fingers but not the additional structural details reported for ESM-3B.
rows.note: This is a qualitative scaling observation, not a measure of the share of interpretable neurons.
rows.check: Same as r21. 'Partial' is not meaningful without a version-linked effect.

rows.subject: ESM variants (aggregate; ESM-8M, ESM-35M, and ESM-3B named in the text)
rows.operation_detail: Examined the relative distribution of labeled feature categories across layer sextiles.
rows.measure: Layer location of labeled feature categories
rows.value: The text reports sequence-derived features peaking in lower layers, structural features peaking somewhat in middle layers and persisting later, and functional features concentrating in later sextiles; it also reports that functional features appear earlier in ESM-3B than in smaller models.
rows.note: The paper presents these as qualitative distributions and gives no neuron-pole job shares.
